summary: Chinese lespedeza is a bushy plant 3 to 5½ feet tall with silvery-green, three-part leaves and stiff, sharp bristles on its older stems. It is the biggest threat to open areas like meadows, prairies, open woods, wetland edges and fields, where it crowds out native plants, forms stands of a single plant, and builds up a large supply of seeds in the soil. Its high tannin content makes it unappealing to livestock and most native wildlife.
history: Chinese lespedeza is native to Asia and Australia. Federal and state agencies brought it to the U.S. in the late 1800s for bank stabilization, erosion control, soil improvement, mine reclamation and animal feed, and it has been escaping from those plantings for many years.
seasons: Small creamy-white to pale-yellow flowers with purple centers bloom in summer, and fruits form in the fall. Animals such as bobwhite quail eat the seeds and spread them.

handling.text: Do not plant Chinese lespedeza. Hand-pulling is impractical because of its extensive root system; mowing plants while they are flowering, as low as possible, for two or three years in a row may help control it.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
